It is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is His words ﴿مثلهم في التوراة﴾ ("their likeness in the Torah"), meaning: their description that they were described with in the Torah, and their description that they were described with in the Gospel. The repetition of the word "likeness" serves to reinforce the statement and to draw attention to its strangeness, and that it functions like proverbs in its strangeness. The phrase ﴿كزرع أخرج شطأه﴾ ("like a seed that sends forth its shoot") is a new, independent sentence, meaning: they are like a seed, and so on. It was also said that it is an explanation of ﴿ذلك﴾, with ﴿ذلك﴾ being an ambiguous reference that does not refer to the qualities mentioned before. It was also said that it is the predicate of His words ﴿ومثلهم في الإنجيل﴾ ("and their likeness in the Gospel"), meaning: and their likeness in the Gospel is like a seed. Al-Farra' said: "There are two possibilities. If you wish, you may say: 'That is their likeness in the Torah and their likeness in the Gospel,' meaning, like their likeness in the Qur'an, so the pause (waqf) falls on 'the Gospel'. And if you wish, you may say: 'That is their likeness in the Torah,' then begin: 'And their likeness in the Gospel is like a seed.'"

The reciters (qira'at): The majority read ﴿شطأه﴾ (shat'ahu) with a sukun on the ta' (ṭāʾ). Ibn Kathir and Ibn Dhakwan read it with a fatha on it. Anas, Nasr ibn 'Asim, and Yahya ibn Wathth'ab read ﴿شطاه﴾ (shaṭāhu), like ʿaṣāhu ("his staff"). Al-Jahdari and Ibn Abi Ishaq read ﴿شطه﴾ (shaṭṭahu) without the hamza. All of these are dialectal variants (lughat). Al-Akhfash and al-Kisa'i said: shat'ahu means its tip (ṭaraf).

Al-Farra' said: "The crop shata' (put forth shoots), so it is mushti' (shooting out) when it emerges."

Al-Zajjaj said: "akhraja shat'ahu" means: it brought forth its growth (nabatahu).

Qutrub said: "al-shat' is other than the ear of grain (sunbul)."

It was also reported from al-Farra' that he said: "It is the ear of grain."

Al-Jawhari said: "Shata' al-zar' wa al-nabat (the crop and the plant put forth shoots), and the plural is ashta'. Ash-ta'a al-zar' means the crop came forth with its shoot (shat'). Then ﴿فآزره﴾ ("then it strengthened it") means: it strengthened it, helped it, and reinforced it." It was said: the meaning is that the shoot strengthened the crop, and it was also said that the crop strengthened the shoot. Among the evidence that shat' means the emergence of growth is the poet's verse:

"It brought forth the shoot upon the face of the earth, and from the trees come branches of fruit."

The majority read ﴿فآزره﴾ (fa-āzarahu) with a long vowel (madd). Ibn Dhakwan, Abu Haywah, and Humayd ibn Qays read it with a short vowel (qaṣr). On the reading of the majority, there is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"In a valley where the wild growth (ḍāll) has strengthened its plants, a passage for armies that are victorious and rejected (?)."

Al-Farra' said: "Ādhartu fulānan ādharan" means: I strengthened him, when I made him strong.

Then ﴿فاستغلظ﴾ ("so it became thick") means: that crop became thick after it had been thin, so ﴿فاستوى على سوقه﴾ ("so it stood firm upon its stalks") means it stood straight on its stems. ﴿سوقه﴾ is the plural of sāq (stalk).

Qunbul read ﴿سؤقه﴾ (sūʾqihi) with a hamza and a sukun. ﴿يعجب الزراع﴾ ("pleasing the sowers") means: this crop pleases its sower because of its strength and beautiful appearance.

This is a parable (mathal) that Allah, the Exalted, struck for the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ): that they would be few at the beginning, then they would increase, multiply, and grow strong, like the crop. For it is weak at the beginning, then it grows stronger from state to state until its stalk becomes thick.

Qatada said: "The likeness of the Companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) in the Gospel is that there would come forth from a people who grow like the growth of the crop, who command what is good and forbid what is evil."

Then He, the Exalted, mentioned the reason for His increasing them and strengthening them, the Companions of His Prophet (ﷺ). He said: ﴿ليغيظ بهم الكفار﴾ ("that He may enrage the disbelievers by them"), meaning: He multiplied and strengthened them so that they would be a source of rage for the disbelievers. The lam (ل) is connected to an implied verb: meaning, He did that in order to enrage. ﴿وعد الله الذين آمنوا وعملوا الصالحات منهم مغفرة وأجرا عظيما﴾ ("Allah has promised those among them who believe and do righteous deeds forgiveness and a great reward") means: He, the Exalted, promised those who are with Muhammad (ﷺ) that He would forgive their sins and multiply their reward by admitting them to Paradise, which is the greatest blessing and the highest favor.

Ahmad and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "They slaughtered seventy camels on the day of al-Hudaybiyah, and when they were prevented from reaching the House, they yearned (ḥanna) as a she-camel yearns for her young."

Al-Hasan ibn Sufyan, Abu Ya'la, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Qani', al-Barudi, al-Tabarani, and Ibn Mardawayh reported it.

al-Suyuti said, with a good chain (sanad), from Abu Jumu'ah Hunbudh ibn Subu' who said: "I met the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at the beginning of the day as a disbeliever, and I met him at the end of the day as a Muslim, and in our case was revealed: ﴿And if there were not believing men and believing women⦘...﴾ and we were nine men, seven men and two women." In a narration in Ibn Abi Hatim: "We were three men and nine women."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿Had there not been believing men and believing women whom you did not know⦘﴾, he said: "When they turned back the Prophet (ﷺ)" ﴿that you might trample them⦘﴾ "by your killing of them" ﴿so that you would be harmed (tazayyalu) (if they were separated)⦘﴾ meaning: if the disbelievers had been separated from the believers, Allah would have punished them with a painful punishment by your killing of them.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others reported from Sahl ibn Hunayf, who said on the day of Siffin: "Accuse yourselves, for we saw ourselves on the day of al-Hudaybiyah, meaning the treaty that was between the Prophet (ﷺ) and the polytheists, and had we seen fighting we would have fought. 'Umar came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, are we not upon the truth and they upon falsehood? Are not our slain in Paradise and their slain in the Fire?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Then why should we give the humiliation in our religion, and return while Allah has not yet judged between us and them?' He said: 'O son of al-Khattab, I am the Messenger of Allah, and Allah will never abandon me.' So he went away enraged and did not remain patient until he came to Abu Bakr and said: 'O Abu Bakr, are we not upon the truth and they upon falsehood?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Are not our slain in Paradise and their slain in the Fire?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Then why should we give the humiliation in our religion?' He said: 'O son of al-Khattab, he is the Messenger of Allah, and Allah will never abandon him.' Then Surat al-Fath was revealed, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent for 'Umar and recited it to him. He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, is it a conquest (fath)?' He said: 'Yes.'"

al-Tirmidhi, Abdullah ibn Ahmad in Zawa'id al-Musnad, Ibn Jarir, al-Daraqutni in al-Afrad, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat reported from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, "from the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning ﴿and made them hold to the word of piety⦘﴾, he said: 'It is: There is no god but Allah.'" In its chain is al-Hasan ibn Qaza'ah. al-Tirmidhi said after reporting it: "It is a gharib (unusual) hadith, and we do not know it except through his narration," and Abu Zur'ah said the same.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Salamah ibn al-Akwa', traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar.

'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat reported from Ibn 'Abbas something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Daraqutni in al-Afrad reported from al-Miswar ibn Makhramah and Marwan something similar, and it is reported from a group of the Successors (tabi'un) something similar to that.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿Allah has certainly fulfilled for His Messenger the vision in truth⦘﴾, he said: "It is the entry of Muhammad into the House with the believers, shaving their heads and shortening their hair." Supplications for those who shave their heads and those who shorten their hair are found in the two Sahihs and others, among which are the hadiths we have already pointed to. It is in the two Sahihs from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, and in them also from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿Their mark is on their faces⦘﴾, he said: "As for it, it is not what they see, but it is the mark of Islam, its composure and its humility."

Muhammad ibn Nasr in Kitab al-Salah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning the verse, he said: "It is the good bearing (samt)."

al-Tabarani in al-Awsat and al-Saghir, and Ibn Mardawayh, with a good (hasan) chain according to al-Suyuti, reported from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said concerning His words ﴿Their mark is on their faces, from the trace of prostration⦘﴾: 'It is the light on the Day of Resurrection.'"

al-Bukhari in his History and Ibn Nasr reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning the verse, he said: "It is a whiteness that covers their faces on the Day of Resurrection."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿That is their likeness in the Torah⦘﴾, meaning: their description is written in the Torah and the Gospel before Allah created the heavens and the earth.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Anas concerning ﴿like a seed that sends forth its shoot⦘﴾, he said: "Its growth is its offshoots (furukh)."

(p-1386) His words: "They are the ones who disbelieved and barred you from the Sacred Mosque" — meaning the disbelievers of Makkah. The meaning of their barring you from the Sacred Mosque is that they prevented you from circumambulating it and from being released from your ʿumrah (pilgrimage), and "the offering (al-hady) detained (maʿkūfan)." The majority (al-Jumhūr) read "al-hadya" in the accusative, as a conjunction with the object pronoun in "ṣaddūkum." Abū ʿAmr, in one narration from him, read it in the genitive, as a conjunction with "al-Masjid," and a governing noun must be supplied: i.e., "from the slaughtering of the offering." It was also read in the nominative, on the assumption: "and the offering was barred." The majority read the ha' of "al-hady" with a fatha and the dal with a sukun; it is narrated from Abū ʿAmr and ʿĀṣim that the dal has a kasra and the yā' is shaddah. The accusative of "maʿkūfan" is a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of "al-hady," meaning: held back.

Al-Jawharī said: "ʿakafahu" means he held him back and stopped him; from this comes "wal-hadya maʿkūfan," and from this comes "al-iʿtikāf" in the mosque, which is confinement.

Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ said: "maʿkūfan" means gathered together.

His words: "an yablugha maḥillahu" — i.e., "from reaching its place of sacrifice," or it is a object of purpose (mafʿūl li-ajlihi), and the meaning is: "they barred the offering out of dislike that it reach its place of sacrifice." Or it is a substitute for "al-hady" as a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimāl). "Maḥillahu" means its place of slaughter, which is where its slaughter is permitted within the Ḥaram. The offering was seventy camels, and Allah, glorified is He, granted them dispensation to make that place, which they had reached — al-Ḥudaybiyah — a place of sacrifice. There is a well-known discussion among the scholars on this in the books of jurisprudence (furūʿ).

"And had there not been believing men and believing women whom you did not know" — meaning the oppressed believers in Makkah. The meaning of "lam taʿlamūhum" is "you did not recognize them." It was said: "you did not know that they were believers, lest you trample them." It may be a substitute for "rijāl" and "nisāʾ," but the masculine was given precedence. It may also be a substitute for the object of "taʿlamūhum," and the meaning is: "lest you trample them" by killing and striking them. It is said: "wataʾtu al-qawm," meaning I struck the people. That is because, if they had conquered Makkah and taken it by force with the sword, the believers who were there would not have been distinguished from the disbelievers, and at that point they would not be safe from killing the believers, so that expiation (kaffārah) would become obligatory for them and disgrace would befall them. This is the meaning of His words: "then there would befall you from them" — that is, from their direction — "maʿarrah," meaning hardship, through what would be obligatory upon them in killing them of expiation and blame. The root of maʿarrah is blame, taken from ʿurr, which is mange. That is because the polytheists would say: "The Muslims have killed the people of their own religion."

Al-Zajjaj said: "Lawlā an taqtulū rijālan mu'minīna wa nisā'an mu'mināti fa-tuṣībakum minhum maʿarratun" — i.e., sin.

Likewise said al-Jawharī, and Ibn Zayd said similarly.

Al-Kalbī, Muqātil and others said: maʿarrah is the expiation for accidental killing, as in His words: "And if he was from a people hostile to you and he was a believer, then the freeing of a believing slave" [al-Nisāʾ: 92]. Ibn Isḥāq said: maʿarrah is the payment of blood money (diyah).

Quṭrub said: maʿarrah is hardship. It was also said: distress.

"Bi-ghayri ʿilm" is connected to "an taṭaʾūhum": i.e., without knowing. The answer to "lawlā" is omitted, and the estimate is: "Allah would have permitted you" or "He would have restrained your hands from them." The lām in "li-yudkhila Allāhu fī raḥmatihi man yashāʾ" is connected to what the omitted answer indicates: i.e., "but He did not permit you," or "He restrained your hands so that Allah might admit into His mercy whom He wills from His servants, namely the believing men and believing women who were in Makkah." Thus He would complete their rewards by bringing them out from among the disbelievers, free their captivity, and remove the punishment that was descending upon them.

It was also said: the lām is connected to an omitted element other than what has been mentioned, and its estimate is: "Had you killed them, Allah would have admitted them into His mercy." The first is preferable.

It was also said: "whom He wills" refers to His servants from among the polytheists who had inclined to Islam. "Had they been distinguished, We would have punished those among them who disbelieved with a painful punishment." Tazayyul means distinction, i.e., had those who believed been distinguished from those who disbelieved among them, We would have punished those who disbelieved. It was also said: tazayyul means separation, i.e., had these been separated from those. It was said: had the believers departed from among them. The meanings are close. The painful punishment is killing, captivity, and subjugation.

The adverbial clause in His words "idh jaʿala alladhīna kafarū" is governed by an omitted verb: i.e., "remember the time when those who disbelieved placed." It was said: it is connected to "ʿaḏḏabnā." Ḥamiyyah means haughtiness. It is said: "Fulān dhū ḥamiyyah," i.e., he has haughtiness and anger. That is, they made it firmly established in their hearts. The "jaʿl" here means placing, and "ḥamiyyat al-jāhiliyyah" is an appositive substitute for "al-ḥamiyyah."

Muqātil ibn Sulaymān and Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān said: the people of Makkah said: "They have killed our sons and brothers, and they enter upon us in our homes, so the Arabs will say that they entered upon us in spite of our noses. By al-Lāt and al-ʿUzzā, they will not enter it upon us." This is the ḥamiyyat al-jāhiliyyah which entered their hearts.

al-Zuhrī said: their ḥamiyyah was their refusal to acknowledge the Prophet (ﷺ) as a messenger.

The majority read "law tazayyalū." Ibn Abī ʿAbla, Abū Ḥaywah and Ibn ʿAwn read "law tazāyalū," and tazāyul means separation.

"Then Allah sent down His tranquility upon His Messenger and upon the believers" — i.e., He sent down calm and dignity upon His Messenger and upon the believers, since the ḥamiyyah that entered the people of disbelief did not enter them. It was said: He made them firm in contentment and submission.

"And He made them adhere to the word of piety" — which is "There is no god but Allah." This is what the majority said, and some added: "Muḥammad is the Messenger of Allah," and some added: "alone, with no partner."

al-Zuhrī said: it is "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful," because the disbelievers did not acknowledge it and refused to write it in the treaty of peace that was between them and the Messenger of Allah (p-1387) (ﷺ), as is established in the books of ḥadīth and sīrah. So Allah specified this word for the believers and made them adhere to it. The first is preferable, because the word of tawḥīd is that by which polytheism against Allah is guarded against. It was said: the word of piety is fulfilling the covenant and steadfastness upon it.

"And they were more deserving of it and worthy of it" — i.e., the believers were more deserving of this word than the disbelievers, and more fit for it than they, because Allah, glorified is He, qualified them for His religion and for companionship with His Messenger (ﷺ).

"Indeed Allah fulfilled for His Messenger the vision in truth." Al-Wāḥidī said: the commentators said that Allah, glorified is He, showed His Prophet (ﷺ) in Madinah, before he went out to al-Ḥudaybiyah, that he and his companions had shaved and shortened their hair. He informed his companions of this, and they rejoiced and thought they would enter Makkah that year. When they returned from al-Ḥudaybiyah without entering Makkah, the hypocrites said: "By Allah, we did not shave, nor shorten, nor enter the Sacred Mosque." So Allah revealed this verse. It was also said that the vision was at al-Ḥudaybiyah. "Bil-ḥaqq" is an attribute of an omitted verbal noun: i.e., truthfulness intertwined with truth. The answer to the omitted oath, indicated by the preceding lām of emphasis, is His words: "You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque," i.e., in the coming year. His words "in shāʾa Allāh" are a conditioning of the promise upon the will of Allah, to teach the servants what they should say, as in His words: "And never say of anything, 'Indeed I will do that tomorrow,' except [with the addition], 'If Allah wills'" [al-Kahf: 23–24]. Thaʿlab said: Allah made an exception in what He knows, so that creation may make exceptions in what they do not know.

It was also said: Allah, glorified is He, knew that some of those who were with him at al-Ḥudaybiyah would die, so the exception occurred for this meaning, as said by al-Ḥasan ibn al-Faḍl.

It was also said: the meaning of "in shāʾa Allāh" is "as Allah wills."

Abū ʿUbaydah said: "in" here means "idh": i.e., since Allah willed, when He showed His Messenger that.

"Secure" (āminīna) is an accusative state of the subject of "la-tadkhulunna." Likewise "muḥalliqīna ruʾūsakum wa muqaṣṣirīn," i.e., secure from the enemy, some of you shaving and some of you shortening. Shaving and shortening are specific to men. Shaving is more excellent than shortening, as is indicated by the authentic ḥadīth of his (ﷺ) supplication for those who shaved, the first and second time, and the speaker says to him: "And for those who shorten," and he said the third time: "And for those who shorten."

His words "lā takhāfūn" are in a place of accusative as a state, or as a new sentence, and in it is an additional emphasis for what was understood from "āminīn." "Fa-ʿalima mā lam taʿlamū" — i.e., He knew what you did not know of the benefit in the peace, because your entry in the year of al-Ḥudaybiyah would have entailed harm to the oppressed believers. It is conjoined to "ṣadaqa," i.e., Allah fulfilled for His Messenger the vision, and He knew what you did not know of it. "Fa-jaʿala min dūni dhālika fatḥan qarīban" — i.e., He made, besides your entry into Makkah as He showed His Messenger, a near victory.

Most of the commentators said: it is the peace of al-Ḥudaybiyah.

Ibn Zayd and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: it is the conquest of Khaybar.

al-Zuhrī said: there was no victory in Islam greater than the peace of al-Ḥudaybiyah.

Indeed, in those two years more entered Islam than had entered before, rather more. The Muslims in the sixth year, which was the year of al-Ḥudaybiyah, were fourteen hundred, and in the eighteenth year they were eighteen thousand.

"He is the One who sent His Messenger with guidance" — i.e., sent with guidance and the religion of truth, which is Islam. "That He may make it prevail over all religion" — i.e., exalt it above all religions, as the emphasis of the noun ("kullihi") indicates. It was said: that He may make His Messenger prevail. The first is preferable.

This was indeed so, by the praise of Allah, for the religion of Islam has prevailed over all religions, and every people of the faiths has been subdued before it. "And sufficient is Allah as a witness" — the bāʾ is superfluous, as has been mentioned in more than one place; i.e., Allah is sufficient as a witness to this manifestation which He promised the Muslims, and to the soundness of the prophethood of His Prophet (ﷺ).

"Muḥammadun rasūlu Allāh" — Muḥammad is the subject and "rasūlu Allāh" is its predicate, or it is the predicate of an omitted subject and "rasūlu Allāh" is an apposition to it. It was said: Muḥammad is the subject, "rasūlu Allāh" is an attribute of it, and "alladhīna maʿahu" is conjoined to the subject, and what follows is the predicate. The first is preferable. The sentence explains what is part of what is testified to. "Those who are with him" — it was said: they are the companions of al-Ḥudaybiyah, but the more preferable is to take it in its generality. "Ashiddāʾu ʿalā al-kuffār" — i.e., harsh against the disbelievers, as the lion is harsh against its prey; it is the plural of shadīd. "Ruḥamāʾu baynahum" — i.e., affectionate and compassionate toward one another; it is the plural of raḥīm. The meaning is that they display toughness and firmness toward those who oppose their religion, and mercy and tenderness toward those who agree with it.

The majority read "ashiddāʾu" and "ruḥamāʾu" in the nominative, as a predicate of the relative clause, or a predicate of Muḥammad and what is conjoined to him, as mentioned earlier.

al-Ḥasan read both in the accusative, as a state or as praise. On this reading the predicate is "tarāhum rukkaʿan sujjadan," i.e., you see them as bowing and prostrating. On the reading of the majority, it is another predicate or a new sentence: I mean His words "tarāhum." "Yabtaghūna faḍlan min Allāhi wa riḍwānan" — i.e., they seek the reward of Allah for them and His pleasure with them. This clause is a third predicate on the reading of the majority, or in a place of accusative as a state from the pronoun in "tarāhum." Likewise, "sīmāhum fī wujūhihim min athari al-sujūd." Al-sīmā means the mark, and it has two dialects: madd (with the long vowel) and qaṣr (without). I.e., their mark appears on their foreheads from the trace of prostration in prayer and the abundance of worship by night and day.

al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: when a man stays up at night he becomes yellowish in the morning, and he made this the sīmā.

al-Zuhrī said: the places of prostration are the brightest of their faces on the Day of Resurrection.

Mujāhid said: it is humility and modesty. With the first — that is, that it is what appears on the foreheads from much prostration — said Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and Mālik.

Ibn Jarīr said: it is dignity (al-waqār).

Al-Hasan said: "When you see them, you think they are sick, but they are not sick." It was also said: it refers to the radiance on the face and the light that appears upon it. Sufyan al-Thawri said the same.

The demonstrative in His words ﴿ذلك﴾ ("that") refers to the noble qualities mentioned earlier. It is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is His words ﴿مثلهم في التوراة﴾ ("their likeness in the Torah"), meaning: their description that they were described with in the Torah, and their description that they were described with in the Gospel. The repetition of the word "likeness" serves to reinforce the statement and to draw attention to its strangeness, and that it functions like proverbs in its strangeness. The phrase ﴿كزرع أخرج شطأه﴾ ("like a seed that sends forth its shoot") is a new, independent sentence, meaning: they are like a seed, and so on. It was also said that it is an explanation of ﴿ذلك﴾, with ﴿ذلك﴾ being an ambiguous reference that does not refer to the qualities mentioned before. It was also said that it is the predicate of His words ﴿ومثلهم في الإنجيل﴾ ("and their likeness in the Gospel"), meaning: and their likeness in the Gospel is like a seed. Al-Farra' said: "There are two possibilities. If you wish, you may say: 'That is their likeness in the Torah and their likeness in the Gospel,' meaning, like their likeness in the Qur'an, so the pause (waqf) falls on 'the Gospel'. And if you wish, you may say: 'That is their likeness in the Torah,' then begin: 'And their likeness in the Gospel is like a seed.'"

The reciters (qira'at): The majority read ﴿شطأه﴾ (shat'ahu) with a sukun on the ta' (ṭāʾ). Ibn Kathir and Ibn Dhakwan read it with a fatha on it. Anas, Nasr ibn 'Asim, and Yahya ibn Wathth'ab read ﴿شطاه﴾ (shaṭāhu), like ʿaṣāhu ("his staff"). Al-Jahdari and Ibn Abi Ishaq read ﴿شطه﴾ (shaṭṭahu) without the hamza. All of these are dialectal variants (lughat). Al-Akhfash and al-Kisa'i said: shat'ahu means its tip (ṭaraf).

Al-Farra' said: "The crop shata' (put forth shoots), so it is mushti' (shooting out) when it emerges."

Al-Zajjaj said: "akhraja shat'ahu" means: it brought forth its growth (nabatahu).

Qutrub said: "al-shat' is other than the ear of grain (sunbul)."

It was also reported from al-Farra' that he said: "It is the ear of grain."

Al-Jawhari said: "Shata' al-zar' wa al-nabat (the crop and the plant put forth shoots), and the plural is ashta'. Ash-ta'a al-zar' means the crop came forth with its shoot (shat'). Then ﴿فآزره﴾ ("then it strengthened it") means: it strengthened it, helped it, and reinforced it." It was said: the meaning is that the shoot strengthened the crop, and it was also said that the crop strengthened the shoot. Among the evidence that shat' means the emergence of growth is the poet's verse:

"It brought forth the shoot upon the face of the earth, and from the trees come branches of fruit."

The majority read ﴿فآزره﴾ (fa-āzarahu) with a long vowel (madd). Ibn Dhakwan, Abu Haywah, and Humayd ibn Qays read it with a short vowel (qaṣr). On the reading of the majority, there is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"In a valley where the wild growth (ḍāll) has strengthened its plants, a passage for armies that are victorious and rejected (?)."

Al-Farra' said: "Ādhartu fulānan ādharan" means: I strengthened him, when I made him strong.

Then ﴿فاستغلظ﴾ ("so it became thick") means: that crop became thick after it had been thin, so ﴿فاستوى على سوقه﴾ ("so it stood firm upon its stalks") means it stood straight on its stems. ﴿سوقه﴾ is the plural of sāq (stalk).

Qunbul read ﴿سؤقه﴾ (sūʾqihi) with a hamza and a sukun. ﴿يعجب الزراع﴾ ("pleasing the sowers") means: this crop pleases its sower because of its strength and beautiful appearance.

This is a parable (mathal) that Allah, the Exalted, struck for the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ): that they would be few at the beginning, then they would increase, multiply, and grow strong, like the crop. For it is weak at the beginning, then it grows stronger from state to state until its stalk becomes thick.

Qatada said: "The likeness of the Companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) in the Gospel is that there would come forth from a people who grow like the growth of the crop, who command what is good and forbid what is evil."

Then He, the Exalted, mentioned the reason for His increasing them and strengthening them, the Companions of His Prophet (ﷺ). He said: ﴿ليغيظ بهم الكفار﴾ ("that He may enrage the disbelievers by them"), meaning: He multiplied and strengthened them so that they would be a source of rage for the disbelievers. The lam (ل) is connected to an implied verb: meaning, He did that in order to enrage. ﴿وعد الله الذين آمنوا وعملوا الصالحات منهم مغفرة وأجرا عظيما﴾ ("Allah has promised those among them who believe and do righteous deeds forgiveness and a great reward") means: He, the Exalted, promised those who are with Muhammad (ﷺ) that He would forgive their sins and multiply their reward by admitting them to Paradise, which is the greatest blessing and the highest favor.

Ahmad and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "They slaughtered seventy camels on the day of al-Hudaybiyah, and when they were prevented from reaching the House, they yearned (ḥanna) as a she-camel yearns for her young."

Al-Hasan ibn Sufyan, Abu Ya'la, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Qani', al-Barudi, al-Tabarani, and Ibn Mardawayh reported it.

al-Suyuti said, with a good chain (sanad), from Abu Jumu'ah Hunbudh ibn Subu' who said: "I met the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at the beginning of the day as a disbeliever, and I met him at the end of the day as a Muslim, and in our case was revealed: ﴿And if there were not believing men and believing women⦘...﴾ and we were nine men, seven men and two women." In a narration in Ibn Abi Hatim: "We were three men and nine women."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿Had there not been believing men and believing women whom you did not know⦘﴾, he said: "When they turned back the Prophet (ﷺ)" ﴿that you might trample them⦘﴾ "by your killing of them" ﴿so that you would be harmed (tazayyalu) (if they were separated)⦘﴾ meaning: if the disbelievers had been separated from the believers, Allah would have punished them with a painful punishment by your killing of them.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others reported from Sahl ibn Hunayf, who said on the day of Siffin: "Accuse yourselves, for we saw ourselves on the day of al-Hudaybiyah, meaning the treaty that was between the Prophet (ﷺ) and the polytheists, and had we seen fighting we would have fought. 'Umar came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, are we not upon the truth and they upon falsehood? Are not our slain in Paradise and their slain in the Fire?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Then why should we give the humiliation in our religion, and return while Allah has not yet judged between us and them?' He said: 'O son of al-Khattab, I am the Messenger of Allah, and Allah will never abandon me.' So he went away enraged and did not remain patient until he came to Abu Bakr and said: 'O Abu Bakr, are we not upon the truth and they upon falsehood?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Are not our slain in Paradise and their slain in the Fire?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Then why should we give the humiliation in our religion?' He said: 'O son of al-Khattab, he is the Messenger of Allah, and Allah will never abandon him.' Then Surat al-Fath was revealed, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent for 'Umar and recited it to him. He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, is it a conquest (fath)?' He said: 'Yes.'"

al-Tirmidhi, Abdullah ibn Ahmad in Zawa'id al-Musnad, Ibn Jarir, al-Daraqutni in al-Afrad, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat reported from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, "from the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning ﴿and made them hold to the word of piety⦘﴾, he said: 'It is: There is no god but Allah.'" In its chain is al-Hasan ibn Qaza'ah. al-Tirmidhi said after reporting it: "It is a gharib (unusual) hadith, and we do not know it except through his narration," and Abu Zur'ah said the same.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Salamah ibn al-Akwa', traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar.

'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat reported from Ibn 'Abbas something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Daraqutni in al-Afrad reported from al-Miswar ibn Makhramah and Marwan something similar, and it is reported from a group of the Successors (tabi'un) something similar to that.

Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿Allah has certainly fulfilled for His Messenger the vision in truth⦘﴾, he said: "It is the entry of Muhammad into the House with the believers, shaving their heads and shortening their hair." Supplications for those who shave their heads and those who shorten their hair are found in the two Sahihs and others, among which are the hadiths we have already pointed to. It is in the two Sahihs from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, and in them also from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿Their mark is on their faces⦘﴾, he said: "As for it, it is not what they see, but it is the mark of Islam, its composure and its humility."

Muhammad ibn Nasr in Kitab al-Salah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning the verse, he said: "It is the good bearing (samt)."

al-Tabarani in al-Awsat and al-Saghir, and Ibn Mardawayh, with a good (hasan) chain according to al-Suyuti, reported from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said concerning His words ﴿Their mark is on their faces, from the trace of prostration⦘﴾: 'It is the light on the Day of Resurrection.'"

al-Bukhari in his History and Ibn Nasr reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning the verse, he said: "It is a whiteness that covers their faces on the Day of Resurrection."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿That is their likeness in the Torah⦘﴾, meaning: their description is written in the Torah and the Gospel before Allah created the heavens and the earth.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Anas concerning ﴿like a seed that sends forth its shoot⦘﴾, he said: "Its growth is its offshoots (furukh)."
